speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP MEETING AT MINISTERIAL LEVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 19, as reported at page 699 of Hansard, I placed before the house the response of the President of the United States to the suggestion I had made in a letter to him representing, as it did, a matter that I brought before the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London. I now wish to report what has taken place since.
Representatives of the nations who are parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade now meeting in Geneva have agreed that a ministerial meeting should be held in the early part of 1963 to consider a program for effective liberalization and expansion of trade in both primary and secondary products. I think I can do no better in this connection than to read from a press communique which will be released today by the GATT secretariat. It says that the contracting parties have agreed that a ministerial meeting should be held in the early part of 1963 to consider such a program to which I have already referred.
-full weight should be attached to the importance and urgency of negotiating solutions to problems of trade in primary products and to the additional trade problems of less developed countries. The proposal that such a meeting should be held was made jointly by governments of the United States of America and Canada.
A precise date for the meeting should be determined by the council of representatives.
The council should be convened for this purpose by the executive secretary at the earliest possible date that he feels that necessary elements exist for arriving at a decision.
In this connection, due weight should be attached to the fact that in order to enable the United States of America to play a full part in a further substantial and early movement for reduction of tariffs and other barriers to trade, it is desirable that the necessary decision to initiate such a movement be taken early in 1963.
Council should at the same time propose an agenda for the meeting of ministers and make adequate preparation for the meeting.
I know the house will appreciate the fact, as it says in the communique, that Canada and the United States jointly proposed in Geneva that this meeting be held. This
decision is directly in line, as I said a moment ago, with the proposal I made for a meeting of like minded nations to consider these trade questions, which received the endorsement and support of President Kennedy last month. Representatives in Geneva have agreed that at this important meeting full weight should be attached to the urgency of negotiating solutions to the problems mentioned therein. That is in entire accordance with the Canadian views, and the government welcomes this decision.
The exact date of the conference will be settled at an early meeting of the GATT council. Arrangements will be made for Canada to be represented at this very important meeting by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and possibly by other ministers as well. I believe that a meeting at this time will have the most far reaching and beneficial results throughout the free world, and will open great possibilities for expanding trade and in consequence expansion in the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should just like to express briefly my own satisfaction in hearing what the Prime Minister has had to say with regard to this world trade meeting as to which our good neighbour to the south and Canada have taken the initiative. Certainly this is a very desirable thing, owing to the simple fact that in the cold war of which we are a part it is impossible to separate the economic aspect, which here vitally concerns the freer exchange of goods amongst the nations and peoples of the earth in order better to meet the needs of people everywhere. In working on the agenda, as the Prime Minister has mentioned, I believe that one of the most important aspects, in addition to the lowering of tariff walls which tend to restrict trade, is the problem of international settlements. In the same way that we were in desperate trouble internally in the thirties with the problem of exchange, so are we now in trouble externally. Here is presented an excellent opportunity to be dealing with this problem in the wider aspect of world trade.
I would also just add this word to the Prime Minister and to his Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is excellent for us to be planning for the long term in relation to trade, but it is also important for us to be planning for the immediate objectives which

GATT Meeting at Ministerial Level we must reach as well. I am sure the government is doing all that it can. I would just add this word in order to impress again the importance of meeting some of these trade problems. We cannot separate our foreign policies from our trade policies, since the real offensive that is directed against us is an economic one.
I am pleased, as I am sure are all of us, that this action is being taken now. Again I would urge that we go forward and bring to the matter the leadership in this regard which I think the people of the world are waiting for, and give some further assurance that we can still live in a day of peace when the development of the world's resources can go forward as it should.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP MEETING AT MINISTERIAL LEVEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of the party with which I am associated welcome the news that a ministers' conference may be held to remove trade barriers between nations and encourage a freer exchange of goods and services among the GATT countries. Hon. members in all parts of the house have expressed their approval of a greater liberalization of trade. I would point out, however, that this objective is not accomplished by having surcharges such as we have had over the last while. I should like to express the hope that by the time Canada attends such a conference we shall go to it with clean hands and with our surcharges completely removed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that the 18 nation committee on disarmament will resume negotiations in Geneva on November 26. General Burns will be returning to Geneva shortly, after consultations here, and will lead the Canadian delegation.
Two questions should receive priority when the 18 nation committee resumes. First and foremost is the urgent need to reach agreement on the cessation of nuclear weapons tests in accordance with the resolution which war recently adopted at the general assembly. That resolution calls for a report to the assembly by December 10. As a result, delegations will need to make an all-out effort.
Second, we believe that early consideration should be given to collateral measures which would reduce international tension and assist the realization of general disarmament. It is particularly important to take full advantage of the lessons of the Cuban experience to ensure that concrete measures are undertaken to reduce the risk of war and diminish the causes of existing tension. This question of collateral measures has been a Canadian initiative from the beginning.

It will also be necessary to proceed as quickly as possible toward agreement on far reaching measures of general disarmament to be embodied in a comprehensive program. As in the earlier rounds of negotiations in Geneva, the Canadian delegation will make every effort to emphasize areas in which positions of the two sides are close to one another and where a wider measure of agreement should be achieved.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to note with satisfaction the announcement of the minister that the 18 member states on the disarmament committee will shortly convene in Geneva. In doing so, I express what I am sure is the general desire of the people of Canada, as well as the membership of this house, that the objectives the government has in mind in this regard will be fully realized. Perhaps, the minister will not mind my saying that it becomes increasingly apparent that the problem is much more difficult than he had first anticipated. Nevertheless, consistent with measures for our security, there will be the strongest desire that progress be made at Geneva this time.
There seems to be some ground for thinking that progress has been made in the matter of the cessation of tests. Certainly if agreement with regard to this matter cannot be reached, it is difficult to conceive how we may look forward realistically in the immediate future to some agreement in the matter of partial or total disarmament.
In any event, the minister may be assured that consistent with our security interests based on the desirability of pinpointing the objects of control and providing for adequate inspection, there will be the strongest desire on the part of the Canadian people that at long last some step may be taken toward progress at this disarmament meeting.

I would also join in giving the Secretary of State for External Affairs assurance of support from our side of the house in his efforts toward this basic objective which must be realized if we are ever going to have peace. I would say this to the minister, that his consistent and persistent efforts in this regard are appreciated. We have awakened out of our lethargy perhaps as the result of the Cuban experience. The point with which I am concerned is that we won round one, but round two might be lost; that is a greater danger to us today than perhaps the crisis which was first precipitated.
Standing upon those principles which are right, upon the need of the basic measures of defence responsibility that we carry, and 27507-3-105
GATT Decision on Surcharges trusting that Canada will lead the way on this question, I may say that she has the respect of the nations of the world and a background that is free from those things which might hinder carrying through this objective. We admit it is an idealistic objective, but it is one which must be reached if reality is to be faced up to at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief statement to make concerning a decision reached in Geneva today by the contracting parties to GATT in respect of Canada's import surcharges. The surcharges were reviewed during the current session of the contracting parties. This provided an opportunity for the Canadian representatives to discuss with representatives of our trading partners the operation of the surcharge measures and the reasons which made them necessary. It also provided an opportunity for other delegations to set out their views about our surcharges fully and frankly. There has been a most useful exchange of views on these matters.
The contracting parties have now taken a decision, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to table that decision. The decision notes the undertaking which has been given by the government, both in this house and to our trading partners, that the surcharges will be removed as soon as circumstances permit. The Canadian delegation was instructed to support this decision, since it is fully in accord with the policy of the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister has asked leave of the house to table a document. I take it there is agreement to that request?

[Editor's note: Text of document referred to above is as follows:]
GATT Decision-Canadian Temporary Import Surcharges
Having received from government of Canada a notification dated June 25, 1962, concerning its imposition, on that date, of temporary import surcharges on numerous products including items bound in parts I and II of schedule V to the general agreement,
Having heard the explanation of government of Canada that the imposition of these surcharges is necessary in order to safeguard Canada's external financial position and balance of payments,
Having also heard Canadian government's explanation of the reason why it took action through the introduction of temporary import surcharges rather than through the introduction of alternative measures,
Taking note of the findings of the I.M.F. concerning the Canadian reserve and payments positions in relation to the incidence of the measures adopted,
Taking note that the government of Canada has begun to introduce longer term corrective measures of a positive and constructive character,
The contracting parties
Express their regret that the government of Canada should have found it necessary to introduce temporary measures inconsistent with article II of the general agreement,
Welcome the beginning made by Canada in the elimination of the temporary surcharges and the stated intention of the government of Canada to eliminate the remainder as quickly as circumstances permit,
Recommend that the remaining surcharges be eliminated expeditiously,
Request the government of Canada to report on action taken to this end to the contracting parties through the council in the early part of 1963,
This decision is without prejudice to the rights of any contracting party under the provisions of article XXIII.

Mr. Speaker, those of us who have had an opportunity to read this statement by the contracting parties will realize that while it is couched in diplomatic language, it seems to be highly critical of the government's action of last June. There are two references in particular which I think should be read into Hansard. One is the notice that the contracting parties have taken that Canada "has begun to introduce longer term corrective measures of a positive and constructive character." Those measures, if they have been taken, have not amounted to very much up to date, in the opinion of some hon. members of the house. It is for that reason

that I think this particular section of the preamble should be brought to the attention of the house and the public.
There is another section that I think should also be read into Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is all in Hansard.

Well, it should be announced publicly; and that is that the contracting parties "recommend that the remaining surcharges be eliminated expeditiously." If I understand the meaning of that adverb it means very soon indeed. In fact, they go on to say they request the government of Canada "to report on action taken to this end to the contracting parties through the council in the early part of 1963." We on this side of the house very much hope the government will be able to do that.

All I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, is that we in our party are delighted that our fellow members in GATT have supported the position taken by this party that these surcharges should be ended at an early date. Although I do not suggest there is any necessary relationship between their decision and the position we have taken, I think the document is a very revealing one. It simply says to the Canadian government, like the small boy caught in the jar, "You have got the jam on your face; if you wash it off we will be prepared to drop the whole thing." I hope the government will act accordingly.

The bay of Fundy has always been considered, since the earliest days, first by Great Britain and thereafter by successive Canadian governments, as Canadian territorial waters. the second reading of Bill No. C-78, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving second reading of this bill I would make a relatively brief statement since, of course, as hon. members who have read the bill know, it contains various sections many of which are technical and there is no general policy running throughout the whole bill, as is sometimes the case. It is therefore much easier to deal with this bill in committee when we can deal with it section by section on the individual matters, and with questions which hon. members will undoubtedly wish to raise, rather than on the general policy of what is an amendment to the Income Tax Act.
The purpose of the bill is to implement the tax proposals introduced in the budget speech on April 10, 1962, and to provide additional administrative and technical amendments that the government believes should be placed before parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Chair hesitates to interrupt the proceedings, but I am afraid the several conferences which are going on are effectively doing so. We should like to hear the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The bill contains a number of provisions which will be of substantial benefit to taxpayers. It is estimated that the total tax revenue given up by the tax concessions to be provided by this bill will be about $128 million on the basis of a full year.
The main income tax proposals which this bill is intended to implement have already been considered, since they were described in the income tax resolution which was before the committee of ways and means last Wednesday. Although all parts of the bill are important, I think general interest will centre upon those parts which implement four major proposals. These are the increased deduction for dependants; a tax reduction for corporations based on increased sales; the right to deduct 150 per cent of increased expenditure on scientific research; and the series of amendments to assist the oil and gas industry.
The additional $50 deduction for dependants will bring important tax savings to all taxpayers with dependant children and other dependants, and will completely relieve some
80,000	taxpayers from payment of income tax.
The production incentive related to increased sales is intended to induce increased production and employment and to stimulate the search for expanding markets. The benefit

Income Tax Act
which will be available to companies engaged in manufacturing or processing will consist of cancellation of 50 per cent of the tax on the first $50,000 of taxable income arising from increased sales and cancellation of 25 per cent of the tax on any additional taxable income arising from increased sales. Both large and small companies will benefit from this measure. Smaller companies will be able to claim the 50 per cent reduction on all their taxable income attributable to increased sales. In fact the cancellation of half the tax on as much as $50,000 of taxable income arising from increased sales will allow the great majority of eligible companies to obtain cancellation of 50 per cent of the tax on all income arising from increased sales.
Implementation of this plan, which will apply to sales at home as well as to export sales, will mean that the large majority of processing and manufacturing companies which increase their sales will be allowed to retain half the taxes they would otherwise be required to pay on their additional income.
The implementation of the proposal to allow corporations to deduct 150 per cent of increased expenditures on scientific research in Canada will provide a powerful incentive for Canadian companies to expand their research. It will also, I am confident, result in a substantial amount of research that is now done outside Canada being done in this country in the future. The deduction for increased research expenditure will apply to current expenditures as well as those of a capital nature. Increased expenditures will be measured by reference to expenditures in a fixed base year. There will, I am sure, be general support of this portion of the bill, which is intended to provide a strong incentive for Canadian companies to maintain and extend their place in the world through advances in research.
The tax concessions for the oil and gas industry are proposed because the government shares the concern of the industry that the pace of exploration for oil and gas is not sufficient to maintain reserves adequate to meet anticipated demands. If Canada is to continue to supply existing markets, let alone expand its markets as we intend, additional reserves will be needed before many years have passed. The tax changes in the bill are intended to secure a more substantial and widespread participation in the oil industry by individuals and companies normally operating in other fields of industry and commerce. By this means we are doing what we can to secure the increased participation of Canadians, in various walks of life, in the ownership and development of this important industry.

In addition to the concessions for the oil and gas industry there are several amendments of benefit to those engaged in mining. The bill also contains a clause to carry out the proposal to change the present deduction for a provincial logging tax into a tax credit equal to two thirds of the provincial tax. Other provisions of the bill which will be of benefit to many taxpayers permit greater portability of amounts set aside to provide a retirement income.
In addition, the bill contains amendments dealing with administration of the act, and a number of amendments which are for clarification or for purposes of cross reference. I shall be glad to furnish whatever information I can concerning all parts of the bill when it is before the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this bill before it goes to committee, and before it is dealt with clause by clause. A complete revision of the Income Tax Act is overdue, as I think most hon. members of this house would agree. I hate to think that it is going to be postponed for several years pending the report of the proposed royal commission on taxation. In mentioning this royal commission I should like to say how sorry I am to have learned about the illness of Mr. Kenneth Carter, the chairman. I am sure all hon. members will hope that he will return to health very soon and be enabled to carry on with this important assignment. However, if the government knows what its objectives are, may I suggest that it should not be difficult for a small group of lawyers and chartered accountants who are familiar with taxation matters to draft a new act in a relatively short time without waiting for the report of the royal commission. I refer to the act as a whole because it leads me into what I wish to say about this bill.
My criticisms of the present Income Tax Act are threefold. First, it is much too complex and complicated for most people to understand. One of the reasons for this situation is the many amendments which have been made to the act over the years in an attempt to cooper up some flaw or other or to grant concessions to some interested party or class of taxpayers. As a result, parts of the act have become almost incomprehensible for the average man to understand.
I say this in all seriousness, and I would think that even the minister would agree with me; because, like him, I have been in professional practice for some years and at one time I had quite a lot to do with income tax practice. Now, however, I find that it

is necessary for me, despite the fact that I used to practise in this field, to retain a tax expert when I have to deal with certain sections of this act. Fortunately in my case I have partners who qualify in that respect, so it is perhaps easier and less expensive for me than for some others. I have in mind particularly such sections as those that deal with designated surpluses and related companies, which perhaps some people are able to understand.
My third criticism is that the law in its present form contains far too many loopholes and anomalies. Periodically government officials bring some of these loopholes and anomalies to the attention of the responsible minister, and sometimes amendments are proposed to this house to correct a particular abuse. But as long as we have an act that is overly complicated and so long as taxation is anywhere near the present levels it will not be possible for busy ministers and a relatively few officials to catch up with the ingenuity of thousands of taxpayers and their advisers in finding perfectly legal loopholes in the act.
I submit that Bill No. C-78 is subject to the three criticisms I have just made of the Income Tax Act itself. This bill is highly complex and complicated; it will be extremely difficult for the average man to understand, and it will provide loopholes for taxpayers to enjoy. Furthermore it will create great difficulties for those responsible for its administration. I have not had the time to make a complete study of the bill, but I did read it carefully last evening while enjoying the results on our bilingual system of television-
You mean the election results.

-of the Quebec election. In order to illustrate the main points I have been trying to put forward I should like to make a few remarks about one section, section 10, which deals with the so-called production incentive. As I understand it, the idea seems to be to grant manufacturing and processing concerns that increase their operations an incentive in the form of lower taxes calculated on the basis of their increased sales. My first criticism is of the concept itself. Most businessmen increase their manufacturing and processing operations to meet increased demands for their products either in the domestic market or for exoprt. I suggest that no sensible businessman is likely to increase his productive facilities and productive capacity merely because he is offered a lower rate of tax on the profits resulting from increased sales. If the business climate is right and it looks as if there will be a
Income Tax Act
continuing demand for their products, most businessmen will try to take advantage of the increased opportunities regardless of the tax rate.
This means that the government should concentrate on doing those things that will create the right kind of economic climate, rather than engaging in a tinkering operation on the Income Tax Act which in my humble opinion will not produce the kind of results that are being sought. But having created the kind of climate in which business can flourish and the economy can grow, and in which there will be more jobs available for those who need them, then if it is desirable to offer incentives to businessmen to increase their productive capacity I should like to put forward two suggestions as examples, and only as examples, which I think would have more real effect than the proposals suggested in this bill. I do this only by way of example.
The first example I should like to give is that manufacturing and processing establishments should be allowed to write off capital expenditures they make to increase their productive facilities against their profits for depreciation purposes at any rate they like to choose. In the long run there would be no loss of revenue to the treasury because people can only write off these assets once, and in the short run increased government revenues arising from increased economic activity in the country would far exceed the temporary reduction in corporation taxes from the firms in question. I believe, and I have said this on several occasions, that far too big a proportion of Canadian resources and Canadian companies is controlled by non-residents of our country, and for this reason I suggest that the kind of proposal I have recommended involving faster depreciation write-offs might be restricted to those companies that are owned by residents of Canada.
The second suggestion I should like to put forward by way of illustration is this. It is important that we should do a great deal more to encourage the establishment of manufacturing, processing and distributing facilities in surplus labour areas. Business concerns might be encouraged to do this if they were offered relief from all corporate income taxes for a three year period in the same way and according to the same principle as in the case of new mining ventures.
I suggest that incentives along these and similar lines would be much more effective than the proposed production incentive contemplated in this bill. This incentive or bonus is based on increased sales, and those responsible for drafting the legislation have gone to

Income Tax Act
some noticeable pains to block certain obvious abuses such as transfers of business between associated and successor companies and the like. But, Mr. Speaker, I can assure the minister that there will be hundreds and probably thousands of businessmen in this country who will find ways of taking advantage of this provision as it is now drafted, ways that are probably not contemplated by the people who did the drafting. In doing so these businessmen will have a perfect right to take advantage of loosely drafted legislation.
The first thing that may happen is that some people may raise their prices, and I cannot believe that it is intended to grant tax incentives to people to raise prices. It is quite true that if businessmen raise prices in order to take advantage of the bonus offered in this section, they may have to spend more on advertising or they may have to employ more salesmen in order to maintain their sales in present volume terms. However, they could do this and at the same time increase their gross sales in dollar terms and therefore get a very nice, fat and unwarranted tax bonus.
Let me give another example. It is almost certain, I suggest, that there will be cases where some company gradually retires from one line of business and this business is picked up by another company. Even if the two companies are connected in some way, it will be very difficult under this legislation for the tax authorities to prevent the second company from claiming the tax bonus offered on these increased sales. I predict, Mr. Speaker, that the benefits of this section will accrue to a much greater extent to the larger corporations, a large proportion of which are controlled by non-residents, than to smaller Canadian owned companies. This is another reason why I have doubts about the wisdom of this particular proposal.
There is also the question of windfalls; and the greatest recent example, of course, is the companies whose export sales in Canadian dollar terms will increase quite considerably because of the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. These companies will not only enjoy increased profits for reasons that were quite beyond their own control, but they are now being offered lower taxes on these increased profits which to me makes no sense whatever.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and for many other reasons to which I am sure the members of this house who are professional men or businessmen could add, I would urge the minister to withdraw this whole section dealing with the proposed tax bonus to manufacturing and processing concerns, 
at least until it has been gone over with a finer toothed comb than I suspect has been used on it up to date. As it stands, I submit it is a bad law and an amateurish way of trying to stimulate business activity in Canada.
Before I resume my seat I should like to urge the minister to do what has been customary on previous occasions before complicated amendments such as are contained in Bill No. C-78 are presented to this house; namely, that the minister or his officials should consult a small group of lawyers and chartered accountants familiar with taxation matters sponsored by the Canadian tax foundation. This is a non-profit organization. These experts, and they are experts, have been willing in the past upon request to provide this kind of service without charge. While they are not usually consulted about the policies involved, which naturally are the sole responsibility of the government, they have been helpful in preventing serious errors in the technical wording of bills or in their drafting. I understand that in this case the minister has not taken the initiative to obtain this kind of advice in connection with the bill, and I urge him to do so while there is still time.

Mr. Speaker, I thought I heard the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) state at the end of his remarks that this is a bad law and that he therefore objected to it.
Even before sitting in the house, I knew that the opposition party always finds wrong what is done by the party in power, while the party in power always insists that what it advocates is for the best.
We, the Social Credit members, do not want to behave in that way.
In the bill now before us, some taxation is acceptable, because we think it is very sensible. On the other hand, there is some we cannot accept. We say, therefore, that this legislation is not wrong in itself, that it contains much that is good. Yet we shall ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) to reconsider some parts of it.
First of all, I shall make a few general remarks. The income tax and the corporation tax legislation is becoming more and more complicated. Today, a whole new booklet is added to the tax legislation.
Mr. Speaker, when such a competent and intelligent accountant as the hon. member for Davenport, who is also a great worker, thinks that our taxation laws are complicated,

I wonder what a simple industrialist, a businessman, an ordinary accountant would think. They must, in my opinion, and probably also in yours, Mr. Speaker, find all that legislation, all those amendments and subamendments extremely complicated.
It has often been said that the more laws there are, the more they are violated. A million laws are violated in the United States, whereas the Lord was satisfied with imposing only ten commandments.
Our laws should be simplified, more particularly those that have to do with income tax, because they are, at this time, the most complex. We should, right now, apply ourselves to streamlining our legislation. That is the first and the only remark of a general character I shall make today.
This is the first time I have the opportunity of commenting on a bill like this, since it is my first session here. If I am not mistaken, the bill is first considered as a whole, and then it is examined section by section.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot but support some sections of this bill, like the one which authorizes larger tax deductions on corporation benefits, that is of 10 instead of 9 per cent, for we know that the amounts collected in this way will be handed to the provinces, in the shape of university grants, at least in those provinces who have signed an agreement to that effect with the federal government.
However, we see that in those amendments to the Income Tax Act the legislator first of all looks after the producer. This applies to legislation from every department, including the Department of Finance.
Under this bill, the producer is to be helped by decreasing his taxes. But one point has been overlooked, and it is that the best way to help him is to supply the consumer with the means of buying his products. If the consumer is unable to do so, even if all taxes paid by the producer were abolished, warehouses, plants or factories will be crammed full as is now the case almost anywhere in Canada.
The best strategy is still to help the consumer absorb the manufacturers' products.
Some provisions of the act would seem to indicate an intention to help the large corporations, but when we consider the long term results, we can see that workers and small people may also benefit from them. For instance, when it is intended to grant tax concessions to those who wish to undertake research one can imagine that such tax reductions will in the long run be
Income Tax Act
beneficial, because they will help improve the quality of products and create new demands on the market, which will develop other productive activities and, consequently, other industries offering jobs to workers.
Mr. Speaker, there is a point we would like to strongly recommend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan), and when the amendments to the Income Tax Act in this regard are submitted to us for examination clause by clause, we will have to object to this particular clause and even vote against it. We wish to give an immediate notice to the Minister of Finance to that effect.
The point I am referring to is this. We approve assistance to Canadian investors for investment in Canadian industry, but we strongly object to tax deductions offered to foreign investors who would like to help us develop Canadian industry.
We object because it would result in a long term loss for us. Let us look at what happened in the past. For years, we were happy to see foreign capital entering Canada. At that time, we had a surplus of foreign currencies in this country. As long as foreign investments kept coming in, we had some advantage, for a time we believed that Canadians derived some advantages from the prevailing situation. But foreign investments lost momentum while the return to other countries of interest and profit payments on capital invested in this country exceeded the annual investments in Canada.
If instead of paying full interest on foreign capital invested in this country in the past, we had those amounts to invest in our industry, we would profit by it just like the foreign companies who invested in our country some 20 years ago. We are paying out more interest to other countries than we are getting foreign capital in the form of investments. Therefore over a long period, we are sure to come out the losers. It is high time that such trend be checked.
It is possible that this may prove difficult for some time. As a matter of fact, we have been finding it difficult for a few years since the very problem I am talking about is the cause of all the financial and monetary difficulties of this government. It is this very problem that forced the present administration to initiate an austerity program.

Income Tax Act
Our foreign exchange reserve has been getting smaller, as we all know. How? Precisely through the outflow from this country of interest and profits on these foreign investments made some 10, 12, 15 or 20 years ago. While we have to bear today the consequences of a mistake made 10, 15, or 30 years ago, we should not put up with that mistake any longer, we should put a stop to it.
Today we are under an austerity program imposed by the government precisely because of a too rapid outflow of foreign exchange in the form of profits paid on foreign capital invested in our country. Consequently, our reserves of foreign exchange have dwindled-

Mr. Speaker, if I understand the procedure in this house correctly-and you can tell me if I am wrong-at this stage of the bill each political party in the house puts forward its general ideas regarding the whole matter of the law, and later we enter into each specific point. My remarks on the bill presented to us are related to some specific points in it.
For example, when I mentioned the variation in corporation tax I said it was something we were ready to accept because it will help education in the province of Quebec. I am now talking about another clause in the bill relating to a deduction of 15 per cent tax in the case of foreign companies investing in Canada. If I am correct in speaking generally on points treated specifically in the bill, then I shall continue.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I am dealing generally with points that we approve and with those we should not approve.
I am pointing out to the government that we are facing an austerity program because, in the past, we have encouraged the investment of foreign capital in our country, while Canadian investments should have been encouraged. Let us put an end at once to this

encouragement of foreign investments in our country.
Also, when the Minister of Finance is proposing to grant tax exemptions of 15 per cent to certain foreign companies which would like to invest in our country, it is my duty to tell him that in ten or 15 years from now, his successor will bitterly regret the mistakes being made this year.
Those are the main points I wished to raise. The points which we are prepared to accept are, for instance, exemptions for those who are doing research, exemptions on company benefits which, in turn, will be handed back to the provinces, to help improve education.
But we are opposed to any assistance to foreign investors.
However, we are not going to content ourselves with opposing that, because in a moment we are going to make a suggestion to the Minister of Finance, in order to compensate for what we want to refuse him. Let him find the Canadian capital needed for the development of our natural resources and our industries, in the Bank of Canada, which is a body coming precisely under the Minister of Finance.
Let him do that, and he will have our support.

I regret I cannot say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I join with others in this house who have agreed with any major part of the bill which is now before us. It is my opinion that, except for one or two concessions to the average taxpayer, about which I shall have a word to say in a moment, this is yet another set of amendments to the Income Tax Act which seeks to give further concessions to those who have already had too many, and to help the large corporations of Canada to make even more out of the development of the people's resources in this country than they have been able to do to date.
There is a little sop to the taxpayer in the increase of the exemption for children by $50. If I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) correctly he told us that several tens of thousands of present taxpayers would fall completely out of the group of those who pay taxes by reason of this small concession.
I am sure the minister would not have made that statement if it were not true. I say that such a statement is a condemnation of our society, a condemnation of the unequal and inequitable distribution of income within it. No government should derive satisfaction from the fact that if you raise an exemption by $50 it will free tens of thousands of people

from paying taxes. This means, in other words, that so many tens of thousands are now living on the very borderline of the minimum income at which taxes are payable.
Moreover, this clearly represents a much more important concession to people with higher incomes than it does to those in the lower income groups. The $50 additional exemption to the man who makes, say, $15,000 or $20,000 a year obviously means much greater reduction in his tax payment than it does to the man who makes only $3,000 or $3,500 a year, who would have hardly any reduction at all. Such exemptions are a proper objective in our society when accompanied by an increase in taxation at the top so that those who can afford to pay higher taxes are not assisted out of all proportion to the help given to those who really need this $50 exemption for a child.
But this, with all its defects, is the only item I see in the bill before the house which is intended to help the ordinary lower income Canadian, who still represents the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people. When we leave that, we come to concession after concession to the corporations of this country.
The minister said that one of the clauses in the bill gives concessions to the oil, petroleum and natural gas industries. May I remind you that the same kind of concession is made, also, in respect of the prospecting and development of mines. When I look at that, I cannot help remembering that in the last couple of days we have had reports in the newspapers of the profits made by some of our large mining corporations.
We learned in recent press reports that in 1953 one of the large nickel corporations of this country, Falconbridge Nickel Mines, made an agreement with the United States government. The United States government had used up its nickel during the Korean war, or had not sufficient reserves of nickel, and wanted to buy a large quantity from Falconbridge. The Falconbridge Nickel Company, according to the press, took the United States government to the cleaners. The nickel was sold at a price of $1 a pound-45 cents more than the market price-and, in addition, the company insisted on a $45 million bonus toward capital expansion to provide for increased production. All this has been brought out in evidence before a senatorial subcommittee in Washington. During that discussion, the chairman of the committee, Senator Symington, said this was outrageous-I am not quoting, now, I am paraphrasing; he said some discussion should have taken place with the Canadian government. One of the witnesses, a Mr. Jesse Larson, informed the committee
Income Tax Act
that there had, indeed, been discussion with the Canadian government before the agreement was signed with Falconbridge in 1953, and that the discussion had taken place with the late Mr. C. D. Howe, then minister of defence production. The late Mr. Howe informed the United States negotiator-this is in the Ottawa Journal of yesterday-that he, the late Mr. Howe, did not want any interference with the private enterprise system. Therefore, he permitted Falconbridge to "take" this country-a large, powerful and wealthy country, it is true but, none the less, an ally of ours; to rob-
Oh, oh.

Yes, rob, because any action of this kind is entirely unjustified. It is utterly wrong to charge the government of another and friendly country almost double the market price of a commodity. Forty five cents out of a dollar which was charged was the amount over the market price. That, I say, without reservation, is robbery by the corporation. The late Mr. C. D. Howe said that was O.K. He would do nothing about it, because to do so would represent interference with the private enterprise system. What a mockery of social morality that is. It is corporations of this kind that the proposed tax concessions will benefit.
Yesterday, in the Globe and Mail, Mr. Speaker, you will no doubt have seen a report that during the first nine months of this year the profits of the International Nickel Company were 23 per cent higher than they were in the first nine months of last year. International Nickel is another mining company to which this bill would give further tax concessions with respect to exploration.
There is nothing in Canada's economy today, from my study of it-of course, I may have overlooked some factors-which justifies added bonanzas to these large corporations, whether they are owned outside or inside Canada. Bonanzas are less justified when they go to corporations outside this country, because we have so much less control; but they are scarcely better when they go to corporations inside Canada making the kind of profits which these reports suggest. Senator Symington said about Falconbridge, for example, that the benefits arising from the deal with the United States in 1953 had enabled the company to increase its profits a thousandfold in 1961 as compared with 1949.
We submit from this corner of the house that the income tax exists partly for the raising of revenue and partly for the redistribution of income in this country, so that those who have not enough may have a little more, and those who have too much have a little less. It is not there for the

Income Tax Act
purpose of giving a little more to those who have too much already, which is precisely, I submit, what this bill does in most of its clauses.
I agree with the hon. member for Davenport in his criticism of the concessions in respect of increased sales. Several weeks ago in the debate on the first resolution, during what I call the non-budget debate, I drew the attention of the committee to the fact that a mere increase in price could lead to the benefit of tax concessions. Similarly, a mere transfer of sales from one company to another, without there being any increase in total sales to the benefit of Canada, could give one of the participating firms the benefit of the proposed tax concession.
I was also interested to read in the business section of the Globe and Mail yesterday that the way in which the companies are defined in the bill before the house with respect to the concessions on increased sales means that a number of companies-not little fellows, Mr. Speaker, but companies like International Nickel, Noranda Mines, and Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada- will find themselves heirs to the tax concessions due to increased sales, because they are companies which manufacture and process as well as mine.
As I said the other day, and if I may repeat it, every time we are told that some concession is made for the purpose of helping the little fellow, my experience from whatever public duties I have had in this country and from studying the economic history of our country has been that although it is made ostensibly to help the little fellow, it is the big chap who really gets the assistance, while the little fellow remains at the wrong end of the stick despite all protestations to the contrary. As the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) correctly stated, this is exactly what will happen with regard to the concessions on increased sales: the big corporations will be able to adjust their personnel, to adjust their finances, to adjust their sales techniques and to adjust their arrangements among themselves in order to take full advantage of the tax benefits.
But, Mr. Speaker, when we go to the hon. member for Davenport, as spokesman for the Liberal party, for suggestions as to what might be done, what suggestions does he propose? He suggests further tax concessions to the corporations. It is true-I must be fair to him-that I heard him say that he suggested these things merely as examples and he may also have said that he would implement them only after there was full employment and full use of present capacity.
Mr. Speaker, may I say that the hon. member for York South did not hear me correctly.

I hoped I did not misrepresent him, but I am glad to be corrected. Am I therefore to understand now that, in place of the kind of tax concessions now in the bill before the house, the hon. member for Davenport is suggesting his tax concessions? One of these was that the corporations should be given a right to write-off capital used in expansion at any rate they pleased. He suggested, that is, that they be permitted depreciation write-offs at any rate they pleased. He pointed out that in the long run this will not really mean a loss to the treasury, because you can only write them off once and eventually taxes will have to be paid on the net income of the company concerned. That may or may not be so in the long run; but I submit that this is merely another kind of gift to the corporations, most of which, with incomes in the large brackets, do not require any more gifts from the public treasury.
Mr. Speaker, when these gifts are made it means that these private corporations, which go about the country boasting of the expansion they have undertaken, of the development for which they are responsible, and so on and so forth, are really expanding their enterprises and carrying on development not at their expense but at the people's expense. They are doing it at the expense of the public treasury. That is why the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), when we were discussing the resolutions the other day, said to this house that these developments in exploration, in drilling and in development of petroleum, of minerals, and the like are taking place at public expense. He added that the public, through the government of Canada, ought to have some say as to the way in which this investment is made and as to the direction in which these enterprises are going.
We are paying-and when I say "we" I mean the people of Canada-for a large part of these exploration and other developments by the tax concessions which have been made. When one looks at the oil, gas and mining companies in this country he finds they already have a capital cost allowance, a depreciation allowance, provision for accelerated depreciation, a depletion allowance by the operator of roughly 33i per cent, and a depletion allowance for income tax on dividends to the shareholders up to 20 or 25 per cent. Now we are adding to the capital cost allowance and to the depletion allowance of these petroleum, natural gas and mining corporations an additional allowance for drilling, exploration, prospecting and

development in the search for oil and minerals. Mr. Speaker, I am not an accountant as are some other hon. members, and even as a lawyer I have not practised in taxation matters and therefore cannot claim to be an expert. However, as I consider the information which I found in a very recent volume on Canadian taxation, by Mr. Perry of the Canadian tax foundation, and as I add up the various allowances which are now given by the Income Tax Act to the corporations and their profits, I wonder what size tax remains to be paid by some of them.
Mr. Speaker, it is our submission to this house and to the minister that some of the provisions of the act which give these concessions to the corporations in Canada are not acceptable, and should not be acceptable, to the Canadian people. It is our belief that if the Canadian people understand, as I am sure they will, precisely what is proposed to this parliament at this time of economic stress, they will disapprove of the kind of gifts given to the corporations of Canada by this bill.
As I have said, we see in it only the increase of $50 in allowances to children which will be of benefit to the average Canadian. We see no decrease in personal income tax in the lower income brackets, and no increase in the tax rate in the higher income brackets, to make up for the added exemption at the bottom. It is our belief that both in justice, in terms of the moral and ethical compulsions of a democratic society, the income tax rate in the lower income brackets ought to be reduced and the income tax rate in the higher income brackets increased in order to promote a more just redistribution of income. Also in terms of the economic need of Canada and of stimulating Canada's economy, a great deal more can be done by releasing the purchasing power of the lower income people by reducing the rate of tax applied to them than can possibly be done by these added concessions involving millions of dollars to corporations which already exploit Canada's resources heartlessly enough.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just want to take a short period of time to answer some remarks made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon). I was interested in listening to what he had to say. He said that he was opposed to the tax incentive based on increased sales because he believed that it will not encourage producers to enter into new lines of production.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might just interject?

Certainly.
Income Tax Act
I do not think I said I was opposed to it. I said that the objective could be achieved in a much more effective fashion.

Well, Mr. Speaker, if my
memory serves me aright, the hon. member said that his party were opposed to this type of production incentive.
No, that is not right.

Certainly, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member and his party are in favour of this type of tax incentive, it is the most lukewarm kind of endorsement I have yet to hear in this house. Mr. Speaker, the facts are simply these. Producers in all parts of the country refrain from going into certain lines of production which are open to them because the profit picture in those lines is not sufficiently attractive to induce them to enter. If there is severe competition in certain lines from abroad that makes it unattractive for them to enter into those lines of endeavour, they do not do so because the energy, the expense and the chance they take by so doing are not made worth while by the opportunities for making a profit which are existent in that particular field. If the profit picture can be made more attractive, then those producers will in many cases enter a line of endeavour which they had not considered sufficiently attractive in the past. However, if the profit picture appears to remain unattractive, or not sufficiently attractive, they will simply leave that job of production to other producers who are more interested in producing that type of goods, and in most instances those producers are located in countries other than Canada.
By substantially reducing the taxes on increased sales, which is what this legislation proposes, this legislation will materially improve the profit picture in many lines of production which, up until now, have not provided a sufficiently attractive profit incentive to induce many Canadian producers to enter those fields. Many Canadian producers will, as a result of this production incentive, be persuaded to enter new lines of endeavour, with resultant increases in production and employment. Since these measures were mentioned by the then minister of finance in the budget of last spring I have talked to many hundreds of Canadian producers at various conferences we have held across this country and I may say that they have been universally enthusiastic about these tax incentives. They say that they will make it possible for them to enter into fields-

When did they see them?

Income Tax Act

These tax incentives were mentioned in the budget of last spring. If the hon. member had been paying attention to what has been going on, he would have been aware of these facts. These tax incentives have been discussed in general by businessmen across Canada and, as I say, they are enthusiastic about them. They feel that many lines which are being produced abroad and which are selling in Canada will now be attractive for them to enter and they intend to do so; and they feel that they will have a very satisfactory production picture and will be able thereby materially to increase employment.
The hon. member for Davenport said he felt that producers might get this tax bonus by simply increasing prices. By saying that, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member shows that he simply is not conversant with the competitive system in this country or any other country. Anybody who is conversant with the competitive system knows perfectly well that producers are selling their products at a price which they consider gives them the best over-all return for their investment. In the competitive system, if a producer increases his price, he automatically loses sales to his competition; if he loses sales to his competition his over-all sales drop; and if his overall sales drop, he will not be eligible for any tax bonus. The matter is just as simple as that. Hence in saying what he has said in opposing this measure, in saying that this tax incentive would be available to producers who simply raise their prices, the hon. member for Davenport is not speaking in accordance with the facts of ordinary commercial competitive life.
During the past few years we have heard the Liberal opposition strongly urge on this government that we should introduce tax incentives. They have used the phrase over and over again. They want tax incentives to increase production and employment. Mr. Speaker, this is a tax incentive which has been worked out with great care, great pains and over a long period of time by the civil servants of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance and other associated departments, and the members of the government. We have worked hard in order to make this tax incentive a simple one, one which can be understood easily, operated easily, and applied easily and which, by its very simplicity and its very soundness, can attract Canadian producers to enter into new lines of production which they Lad not found profitably attractive previously. Under these circumstances when this new legislation is passed, as we hope it will be, many producers will find the profit incentive

attractive enough to induce them to get into these new lines, produce more goods and provide more jobs. But having worked this measure out and presented it to the House of Commons and having had an enthusiastic response for it from businessmen in every part of Canada, what do we find? As the hon. member for Davenport maybe does not know, in that matter we are unlike the government of the party to which he belongs. They never bothered holding conferences across Canada, in all parts of Canada with the businessmen and producers of Canada so that they could find out, so that those producers and businessmen could discuss business matters with members of the government.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I should like to know which government I am supposed to be a member of.

I said "the government of the party to which the hon. member belongs". I hope he can understand those simple terms. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the government that ruled this country-and I say "ruled" advisedly-for 22 years.
Twenty two years of prosperity.

-never bothered to go across Canada and invite businessmen in, or go to them on their home ground and discuss business conditions with them in order to find out their problems, to outline what the government can do to help them. These businessmen in the conferences that we have had with them since these tax incentives were introduced in the budget of last spring, have expressed great enthusiasm in all parts of the country for these tax incentives. However, because we have brought in something that is going to increase production materially, and to increase employment materially, that is something that this Liberal opposition automatically opposes because, as I have said over and over again, they are not in favour of anything that increases production and employment. They want things that will not increase employment and production. As I have said before and say again, the only thing in which they are interested is increased unemployment, because they think it will enhance their chances of getting into office at some future time. Hence we can well understand the official spokesman of the Liberal opposition standing up in this House of Commons and vigorously opposing a tax incentive measure which will do exactly what he has advocated we do, namely increase production and greatly increase employment in this country of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure it must be a matter of great regret to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) who has the responsibility for this bill in this house and indeed for the matters that are of the utmost importance to the welfare of this country, that his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) should have shown so little comprehension of the measure now before the house and which the house is being asked to approve, and that he should have had to listen to that colleague refresh the memory of the house on the fact that the unemployment rate since the Minister of Trade and Commerce became a minister of the crown has almost doubled throughout the whole of the period since that time.
Oh, oh.
Oh, nonsense; absolute nonsense.
And the major part of that increase was due to the incompetence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Of the previous administration.
-and the wrong policies followed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his unwillingness to deal with matters of policy as they related to the subject of trade-
I never knew you were a comedian before.

*-and was contributed to by the present Minister of Finance's predecessor in office because of his stubborn unwillingness to deal with the financial policies of this country in a responsible way and to adopt policies that would bring prosperity to Canadians. May I tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce in case he does not know it, that businessmen and others concerned with production in this country had a very good relationship with the former government and they had a good relationship, among other reasons, because-

A few tycoons did, but the ordinary little businessmen were brushed aside, and you know it. Only Texas oil men like Clint Murchison did. He had a very good association with your government, but not the little businessmen.
Now that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made a second speech-
He will have lots more too.

may I say I am happy to have him interrupt me because-
Income Tax Act
There is just so much nonsense one can listen to.

-if there is anything that demonstrates the weakness of the present government it is the calibre of the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am quite content that his remarks should go on Hansard in the course of my speech so that they can be evaluated by persons who read Hansard.
Nobody reads your speechesr George.
That may well be.
They will go unknown.

That may well be; but there will be persons interested in reading the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce who will read his remarks in Hansard, and if they do I am quite sure they will see what is wrong with the present government.
I want to continue the remarks I was about to make when the Minister of Trade-and Commerce interrupted me. I would point out to all hon. members that relations between industry, business and other people engaged in production in this country, and the former government, were very good and for an obvious reason. When those representatives of business or production did deal with the government of that day they found they were dealing with men-I am referring particularly to the holder of the office of minister of trade and commerce as it was then as compared with now-men who understood their problems and who were capable of listening and finding out exactly what the problems were.
And then doing nothing.

When representations were made to them they were capable of assessing and evaluating those representations and taking the kind of governmental decisions required to meet any difficulties that existed. So when the Minister of Trade and Commerce tries to misinterpret the speech

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Don't be so modest, George.

I have no occasion to be modest about the member of the former government who held the office of minister of trade and commerce, and I think any businessmen or other thoughtful persons who study government in Canada will share that view and will not think me immodest in making claims of competence for him.
I regret very much that when we are dealing with a matter of significance to industry generally, to employment generally and to the welfare of this country the present Minister of Trade and Commerce should

Income Tax Act
have sought to misinterpret the remarks ol the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon). That hon. member dealt with the taxation measure before the house and attempted to point out what he thought were its weaknesses and how best it could be improved. What better method is there of dealing with legislation that comes before the house? The attempt of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to indicate that businessmen of the country had seen the bill and and approved it is simply misleading to this house.
They were familiar with the principle of the bill.

The bill itself bears date of November 12. Actually it was made available on November 13 and has been in circulation for two days. That is quite within the rules and I have no complaint. For my own part I regret that I have not had a better opportunity of studying it more thoroughly because in my view it is a measure that deserves thorough study. Be that as it may, the Minister of Finance is quite within the rules in presenting it on short notice. I have no objection for another reason: The bill has been so long in coming before the house since the presentation of the first budget or the budget of 1962 that I am certainly not going to raise any objection now if notice is a bit short. As a matter of fact one of the criticisms I have of the government is that they did not proceed with this measure and permit debate on the budget when the resolutions on which this bill is based were first introduced. I have sharp criticism of them on that point, but I do not wish to digress in that regard at the present time.
In dealing with the principle of the bill today the Minister of Finance indicated in his remarks that, for purposes of discussion of its principles, the bill could be subdivided into four main parts or subject matters. I think that is a fair assessment. I wish merely to take a few moments to deal with one of the four parts, the oil and gas industry. At the resolution stage the remarks of the minister on this subject, as he admitted with some modesty, were not very full. I read Hansard again on this subject a few minutes ago and I found that he said he was not an expert on the oil and gas industry and therefore was not able to give the kind of explanation that was being sought at that time. However, he was kind enough to indicate that he would make further reference to the matter on second reading and presumably in the committee stage as well. I am no expert on the oil and gas industry either.
IMr. Mellraith.]
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is an expert in the gas industry.

Yes, I know he is; he is an expert in everything. I am one of those who are not overly enamoured of experts on all these subjects. I want to find out about these things myself and then do the best I can with them. I believe the Minister of Finance spoke from a carefully prepared statement today, and as I understood his remarks he sought to make it clear that the part of the bill having to do with the oil and gas industry was designed to meet the concern so widely evident in the country about the lack of adequate discovery of new reserves, and also to deal with the problem that arises due to the fact that the present taxation structure does not provide sufficient encouragement to Canadian companies to expend their available funds on oil and gas exploration.
I want to say at once that I am in complete accord with those purposes, if I have understood them correctly. If there is one thing that must be very clear to all concerned it is that, if we are to expand our markets in the years ahead we must do the exploration work long in advance of expanding those markets, and we must spend the time and the money-it is expensive-in exploration now. My criticism of the present government in this respect is that they did not take this action soon enough in respect of the oil and gas industries. If one looks at the statistics having to do with additions to reserves or the discoveries of new fields or new pools in old fields for the last 11 years, he will find there is a rather alarming decrease in those new discoveries. I suggest respectfully those are the figures that must be taken into account in assessing the need for this tax legislation as it affects the oil and gas industries, and not the total reserves. When you take the total reserves, you are dealing in many cases with revisions of previous estimates and extensions to known fields. In other words, they are somewhat misleading.
I do not intend to give the figures in detail, but they show continuously from the year 1954 onwards a considerable downward trend, with the exception of one year, 1959, and I believe that was the year of the Swan Hill discovery. There is an explanation for that one figure, in any event. However, leaving out that one figure there is a fairly sharp and consistent downward trend in the statistics relating to these discoveries of new fields, or new pools in old fields. This points up rather sharply the need for more exploration work now.
As recently as 1948, I think, although I have not had the opportunity of looking up

the figures, we were importing some 88 per cent of our oil requirements into this country. Today, we are producing something of the order of 80 per cent of our requirements. These figures, as I say, are given without having had the opportunity of checking them, but I believe them to be approximately accurate. I should like to make it very clear that the government is to be encouraged to proceed with measures that will help the industry spend more of its funds in the exploration of new fields.
There are one or two other peculiar anomalies in the existing legislation. There is the matter of the effect of the tax legislation, in the United States and Canada combined, which makes it more advantageous for United States companies to enter this field than for Canadian companies to spend their money in it. This is a condition that is quite undesirable. I believe that the members in all parties would wish that everything be done to enable Canadians to do their share of this development work. As I read the bill, quite frankly I find the sections complicated and I am not absolutely certain that they accomplish what is sought to be done by them. I have some reservations about that. However, be that as it may, we are dealing with the principle now and we hope the principle will achieve these two objectives of increasing exploration and increasing Canadian participation in this exploration. These two ends are desirable, and I wanted to record my views in connection with them.
In so far as the sections of the bill are concerned, I must say that to some extent I have to trust the minister as to what they actually mean, because to discern either the principle or the precise meaning of the sections from a reading of the bill is somewhat difficult. However, there can be more said about that at the committee stage. At this stage, I merely wanted to get on the record something that I thought would be definitive on this point, and to make clear what I believe to be the position of great numbers of Canadians on it.

Mr. Speaker, not being an expert it will not be necessary for people to look through a 30-minute speech in order to ascertain what I have to say on this subject. First of all, I want to be on the record as being in favour of any incentive that is given to exploration and research in this country. I believe it is very important to our way of life that we have the utmost in research and exploration, whether it be in gas and oil, minerals or in the ways and means of increasing production on the farm
Income Tax Act
or in the forest. I feel it is commendable that legislation should be introduced to create an incentive in that regard.
I do think, however, in connection with secondary industries that we have the cart before the horse. I believe that secondary industries-I have been in business myself- are dependant on markets. I am wholly convinced that our markets are basically domestic markets when we have a balance of trade between this country and any other country in the world through unilateral or multilateral trading. If, in fact, our markets are domestic markets, I believe an incentive must be given to the individual to produce for these markets, and these markets must be increased through purchasing power in the hands of the individuals who compose the potential markets. Today, these people lack the purchasing power.
I believe that if we, as a group of individuals in this House of Commons, can devise ways and means of increasing our markets in Canada by fiscal and monetary policies, then we are going to create incentives, perhaps through these tax reductions on sales as outlined by the minister. It seems to me it must be apparent to each and every one of us that a person who is getting all the things he can relatively take out of life is not likely to be a market for any goods or services. The men and women in this country are limited in the amounts that they can take unto themselves in the way of goods and services. The millions of dollars that some individual may have do not mean he can eat any more than so many pounds of food, drink any more than so many bottles of wine, occupy more than one seat in an airplane or a train or drive more than one car at a time. These things are fundamental and I think we must keep them in mind when we are dealing with this situation of markets and incentives.
To my mind this is the incentive we should be looking for. With the increased purchasing power of our people they can buy the things they need and increase their standard of living. If we keep this in mind we shall be much further ahead than trying to start at the opposite end by encouraging people to produce just because they are going to make greater profits out of a small production. The production output of any producer should be for the use of the consumer, and if the Canadian consumer is not using everything he should be, then we must seek to improve his lot.
I would like to see the government go direct to the Bank of Canada in order to devise means by which the purchasing power of the Canadian people can be increased. When their purchasing power is increased, this

Income Tax Act
would be a source of capital for hospitals, schools, roads, bridges, wharfs and all the things we need so badly. The people themselves will become the market and the incentive for the production of goods and services.
