house that if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) takes the floor he will conclude the debate.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, I may have been caught slightly off guard as I thought the hon. member for Cariboo would have spoken at greater length. A little earlier I listened to an exchange taking place between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Davenport. I have no desire to become involved in their quarrel as to which of their parties has been the best friend to big business, but in the light of the remark made by the minister about the enthusiasm he found among businessmen with whom he had discussed his tax incentive proposals, I wish to ask him whether he has yet found anyone in the country who was not enthusiastic about a reduction in his taxes? That, in part, might explain the enthusiasm which the minister met.
When he was moving second reading of the bill, the Minister of Finance suggested that he found some difficulty in finding just what was the principle of it. I take it that the basic principle is to amend the Income Tax Act, and that principle was neatly outlined by my colleague from York South, earlier in the debate. In view of the fact that the Minister of Finance seems, on occasion, to have some fondness for biblical quotations I would suggest for his consideration what I think would be an appropriate text expressing the principle of the bill. It is "To him that hath shall be given and to him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath." For that reason my concern is not so much with what is in the bill but with what I do not find in it. If I might make another biblical reference I would suggest that this bill tends to continue the distinction between those who sit at the table above the salt and those who sit below it.
As the hon. member for York South has suggested, all it contains are one or two small crumbs for the people who sit below the salt and, generally speaking, I would say that most of the people who sit below the salt are people whose income comes directly from a salary or a wage.
It is fair to say that the greatest omission in this bill is the fact that there is little in it for those people who constitute the vast

majority of the taxpayers of Canada and, as has been previously suggested, its terms and provisions are almost entirely confined to providing things for those people whose income comes from business and investments in one form or another.
As has been the case on previous occasions when we were dealing with this question, my concern is with the specific limitations that are found in the Income Tax Act which prohibit those persons whose source of income is a wage or salary from making deductions from their taxable income, deductions which are allowed to many other categories of people within the country. This is a matter which has been discussed on many occasions previously when we were dealing with proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act. In fact this is at least the fifth session during which I have raised the question I have in my mind with respect to the kind of omissions found in bills presented by ministers of finance, and I regret that on coming back to the house after an absence of some four years I find myself once again in the position of having to bring forward an argument related to this basic discrimination that is being carried forward year by year in the Income Tax Act. The present bill does nothing to remove that discrimination.
I had intended to say something about this on the resolution stage, but at that time I yielded to the suggestion of the Minister of Finance who said he would like to get the matter beyond the resolution stage. Now I should like to go into the question in some detail but I notice that the hour has now reached five o'clock and I shall not be able to express at this time what I have in my mind. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to call it five o'clock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It now being five o'clock the house will proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely private bills.

The house in committee on Bill No. S-4, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company (without amendment)-Mr. Ormiston-Mr. Paul in the chair.
On clause 1-Line of railway authorized.

Mr. Chairman, we had quite a lengthy discussion on this bill in the standing committee where some of us endeavoured to get certain information that we felt was necessary for a study of the desirability of this project. I was particularly interested in having a representative from the C.N.R. brought before the committee to give us

information as to whether or not, in a completely efficient way and without any prejudice to the efficient operation of the company, the C.N.R. could handle the output of this company. However, the majority of the members of that committee decided that this should not be done, and the motion was turned down. I think it is the duty of members of this house, particularly at a time when the C.N.R. is running a substantial deficit, to look very carefully at any proposal which is likely to reduce the potential revenues of the C.N.R. and thereby increase the burden on the public purse. For this reason many of us were anxious to have representatives of the C.N.R. come before the committee. However, that proposal was turned down and the bill has been reported back to the house. What faces us today, therefore, is the bill itself.
Some of us have a particular reason for questioning the desirability of building more branch lines at a time when the railway companies are determined to tear up in a rather wholesale fashion, from one end of this country to another, many of the branch lines which are already in existence. I received in my mail today a document which shows that the C.N.R. itself is now determined to take up 74 miles of railway line within my own constituency. It is just a further indication of the pattern which is developing and I, certainly, shall resist this kind of thing.
In such an atmosphere it was, I think, understandable that we should question very carefully whether or not a duplication of services was required in this instance when other users of freight facilities in this country are being deprived of the use of even a single railway.
Having said that, I wish to make it clear that this industry is of great importance to the province of Saskatchewan. The proposed railway line, when it is in operation along with the existing C.N.R. line, will take out the product of a very large potash development being operated in Saskatchewan by the International Minerals and Chemical Corporation. Potash, as hon. members well know, is a constituent of fertilizer which is required in large areas of the world. It is a commodity which is in great demand and in short supply. This would mean a large payroll for people working on the project in this area of Saskatchewan. It will mean some mineral development and, altogether, it is most welcome. I am sure the people of Saskatchewan will want to see everything done which will maximize the efficiency of operation of this mine.
I think the witness for the company gave us very valid reasons, from his standpoint,
Canadian Pacific Railway why this line should be built. He pointed out that there was a shortage, as far as any one company was concerned, of rail cars suitable for the transportation of potash and that it would increase the efficiency of the company as well as the availability of potash on short notice if there was an opportunity to take advantage of the facilities of both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. I think the company itself made an excellent case for the building of this additional railway line. That does not detract at all from my desire at that time to hear a representative of the C.N.R. I do not think that any project, if it is a sound one, can be hurt by having the fullest amount of information placed before the committee. However, the majority of the members said no, and that being the case we are faced in this house with Bill No. S-4 to enable the C.P.R. to build 15 miles of railway line in Saskatchewan to Bredenbury for the purpose of taking out salt. We on this side of the house will support the bill and expedite its passage so that these facilities may be available to the company as quickly as possible.

I, too, am a member of the committee which went into the bill now before us. I should like, in the strongest possible language, to protest against the manner in which we have to pass an important piece of legislation on the basis of information which is totally inadequate to allow for an intelligent and reasoned decision.
Several simple facts are to be found in the evidence. In the first place, the Canadian National Railways is already serving this mine. Second, the spokesman for the company informed us, or told us in answer to questions, that this matter had been discussed with the C.N.R. and that that railway company felt they could handle the situation themselves-that another line was not required. Added to those simple facts, I wish to place on record two more considerations namely, the present dismantling of branch lines, particularly on the prairies, and the fact that we all have copies of the MacPherson report which urges upon this country and upon this parliament the rationalization of our transportation system and opposes the continuing proliferation of branch lines.
In spite of this, we are to give authority to build a duplicate line. We were not given any information as to whether such a line was needed. The majority of the committee decided the C.N.R. should not be invited to tell us if they believed they could handle the traffic. So we are being asked to permit the building of a duplicate line in an area where branch lines are continuing to be pulled up merely on the submission of a spokesman

Canadian Pacific Railway
for the company which, as far as I am concerned, meant simply: the more carriers we have, the happier we shall be. Of course, from his point of view, if he could have every railway and trucking company in Canada coming to his mine so that he could pick and choose between them, he would be happiest of all. But that would not serve the interests of Canada. All we have before us is a statement by a spokesman of the company that they do not want to have to rely upon one carrier only. We have that, and we have another statement by a spokesman of the Canadian Pacific Railway that they think there will be enough business for both railways and that they, also, would like a chunk of it.
I can think of nothing less informative or less valuable than that kind of information, or evidence, upon which to make a decision. With the C.N.R. in deficit all the time, having a line already in existence to service this mine, and in the absence of any evidence why it cannot continue to serve the mine in the future, we are asked to take a step which would necessarily reduce the possible revenue of the C.N.R. and, thereby, increase its deficit. This is why I asked in committee that we should have an opportunity to learn more about the contract between the company and the C.P.R.-that we should know more about the proportion of production which would be shared by these lines.
That is why the hon. member for Assini-boia asked that a spokesman of the C.N.R. come and tell us what the C.N.R. think about the necessity of the situation. Both of those requests were refused, and in my opinion, and I say this with great conviction, this committee is really not able to make a reasoned judgment on this bill. This committee will simply have to act on it, if it votes in favour of it, by accepting the proposition put forward by hon. members in the committee, that we should assume that if the C.P.R. come and say that they want this duplicate line, then they should know what they are talking about. If this is the assumption, then I say to this committee of the whole what I said to the standing committee, why bother us? Why not just let them decide whether or not they want to build, if we are merely to accept their statement about the necessity? It is our business, as I see it, to go into that matter, and we have not done so. The standing committee did not do so, and in my submission this committee is not in a position to make a decision which has any intelligent relevance to the needs of the situation.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to speak for long. This is my first experience of a bill before a standing committee, and I feel very

unhappy indeed. I gather that I can look forward to a great many similar experiences in the future. I say, this committee and this parliament are not in a position intelligently to decide on this bill, because we have not got the information which must form the basis of an intelligent decision. I have not any doubt in my mind that the way in which hon. members jumped to the defence of the bill in the standing committee was due entirely to the fact that the indestructible, infallible and omnipotent Canadian Pacific Railway company appeared as the benefactor of the bill before parliament.

speechtext: This bell always rings true.
It always rings, too.

As one who had something to do with this company's coming into Saskatchewan, and as one who spent a great deal of time and effort in encouraging them to come into Saskatchewan, surely no one will accuse me or those associated with me of trying to hinder their development. However, that is a totally different thing from using that as an excuse for asking parliament to vote on a bill without the kind of information upon which parliament can make a rational and intelligent decision. I think it was Will Rogers who once said that you could walk across Saskatchewan with one foot on the C.P.R. line and the other one on the C.N.R. As we look back now, we think there was some pretty bad planning with reference to railway construction in days gone by. The people of Saskatchewan are now paying for this, because at the moment there are a large number of applications to haul up many of these lines as some of them are duplicate services and the railways now claim they are unnecessary. This means that communities which have been established, businesses which have been located and grain handling facilities which have been built along the lines, are going to become virtually worthless if they are pulled up. Surely, if we cannot correct the mistakes of the past, at least we can learn from them and not commit the same mistakes in the future. There is nothing quite so stupid as to keep on making the same mistake.
Here is an application to duplicate a line which is already in operation, a line which
Canadian Pacific Railway serves a potash mine. I submit that the representatives of Canadian National Railways should have been called. I should like to see this committee refer the bill back to the standing committee and insist that a representative of the Canadian National Railways be called to say whether or not, in the opinion of that company, it would experience any difficulty whatsoever in servicing the potash mine operated by the International Minerals and Chemical Corporation (Canada) Limited. If they express some doubt that they could handle the very heavy volume of traffic which will emanate from that mine, then this committee of the whole would be perfectly justified in giving its consent to the construction of an additional line by the Canadian Pacific Railway. But, Mr. Chairman, I submit that if the Canadian National Railways are convinced that they can handle this volume of traffic, then it should be given sufficient time to show whether or not its contention is borne out by the facts. If parliament in the future finds that it is not able to handle that traffic, surely that would be time enough to authorize the construction of a second line.
What we are being asked to do here is to authorize the construction of a line to duplicate a line already in existence, which would have the effect of dividing the traffic when that division of traffic may be totally unnecessary. The question is not whether we want to develop an industry in Saskatchewan: we are all interested in developing industries anywhere in Canada. What we are anxious to do is to avoid the mistakes of the past with regard to constant duplication of railway lines, which can only break up the traffic. If the traffic is divided so that the volume of traffic which each railway gets is not sufficient to cover the operating and capital costs, it means that the burden has to be borne by shippers on other lines, and this pushes up freight rate and other costs.
In Canada, as the MacPherson report has pointed out, one of the reasons for our high freight rates and for the deficits which particularly the Canadian National Railways have experienced, is the obligation to carry a great many unremunerative lines. We in this House of Commons ought to know whether we are simply constructing another unremunerative line or a line which, if it does become remunerative, may make unremunerative the C.N.R. line which is there. I submit that the issue at this time has nothing to do with the development of industry. The issue at that time is whether or not this house has been given the information to which it is entitled and upon which it can base a reasoned decision on an extremely important matter. For us merely to jump up and vote for the bill

Canadian Pacific Railway because an hon. member stands up and says, "If you vote against this bill this will be interpreted in the country as being opposed to the development of an industry in Saskatchewan" seems to me is a complete attempt to escape the responsibilities which lie upon members of the house.
As members of the House of Commons we have a responsibility to decide whether we are going to authorize a duplicate line. I for one have not been given sufficient information upon which to make that kind of decision, and I am convinced the committee was not given .sufficient information.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just resumed his seat and the hon. member for York South brought forward a seemingly frightening indictment about what seems to me to be an ordinary procedure of this house. Surely the simple fact is that the Canadian National Railways did not oppose the bill before the committee. The Canadian National Railways have a right to appear before the committee and to state their views. They had notice of the committee meeting. The notice is widely given in government documents or in public documents. Surely the silence of the Canadian National Railways is more eloquent than are any speeches against this development.

It has been intimated by some of the hon. members who have spoken that there was something improper or high handed on the part of the committee. The opposition are always very ready to remind us that this is a house of minorities. The composition of the committees reflects the composition of the house. The party of the government is a minority on the committee as well. We were there. We voted. I think that the votes were fair. We took all the time that was necessary to hear the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Assini-boia. The violence of the protestations of the hon. member for Assiniboia today I think perhaps arise from the fact that he forgot himself for a while the other day in committee and reverted to his political antecedents.
The Conservative party is a party of free enterprise. This was an application by a free enterprise organization to build what amounts to little more than a spur line. If it had been six miles in length, they would not have had to be before the committee. Their spur amounts to 12 miles. They brought forward impressive reasons why-
Fifteen and a half miles.

The hon. member says it is 15J miles. That is not much longer. I can still walk it. The company and

the railroad brought forward impressive arguments as to why it was needed and as to why the C.N.R. could not supply the service required. These arguments included, first, the rapidity of shipping. When the product of this mine, namely potash goes out, it must go out rapidly. The next argument was the available supply of box cars. They felt that even though the C.N.R. had all the products of the mine to ship, it could not supply the box cars which might be required. They also said that it was economical from the point of view of market destination to have available to them shipping by both lines. I should like to revert for just a minute to the problem of box cars. Some hon. members seem to take the attitude, "Oh well, if there are 100 more hopper cars, they could handle all this shipping".
The point of this is that the cost of the project is $668,000 and the cost of a hopper car is something like $21,000. Less than 33 hopper cars are the equivalent of the cost, and 33 hopper cars added to any railroad system could not provide the additional shipping facilities required by the company. The argument is logical. It was a free enterprise argument. There was nothing underhanded and nobody was bludgeoned or overwhelmed by the appearance of the C.P.R. This bill should be passed now.

I will not take more than a minute, Mr. Chairman, to say to you and to the members of the committee that the witnesses in reply to questions, admitted that the C.N.R. could rent hopper cars from the C.P.R. Spokesmen for the company informed the committee that they have some hopper cars which they could and would bring down to Esterhazy. In my experience I have seldom heard a lamer reason for building anything like what is now before us than to suggest that you must build it because one of the railways does not have all of the hopper cars necessary. It is well known that cars on freight trains-and I refer to every sort of car-interchange among railways all the time, or run from one line to another all the time. I wanted to put on record that this hopper car argument was made but that, in my submission, on the evidence it is not anything like a weighty argument.

I regret that the occasion has arisen whereby we have this bill before us now and presumably will have others in the future upon which we will have to make comments. Our reasons for expressing that regret have been enumerated on a number of occasions.
There is the question of the custody, maintenance and welfare of the children. There is the question of whether or not there is a prohibition against engaging in a debate of that sort or whether we have any authority or jurisdiction with regard to such matters. There is the question of alimony payments and whether or not we have any right to deal with it. There is the question of the exorbitant charges petitioners must incur in presenting bills of this kind. There is the very important question of whether or not matters of private concern to individuals should be the subject of debate and consideration in parliament.
But the bill is before us and I presume other bills will come before us and therefore we have to express our thoughts with respect to each one, as has been the case in the past couple of years, in the hope that by expressing these thoughts and ideas we may be able to bring about some changes. The alternatives to the present procedure have also been enumerated on a number of occasions. We have even gone so far as to take cognizance of the penchant of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for the appointment of royal commissions in the hope that he would appoint a royal commission to deal with this question. But such is not the case. No changes have been made and therefore we must proceed to deal with these bills on the same basis as in the past few years, particularly in the last parliament.
The bill seeks in principle to dissolve a marriage between two individuals, and I think that is the sole principle involved here. As always I will try to keep within the bounds of the rules in any comments I make. But in seeking to discover whether or not we want to dissolve the marriage I think we have got to determine whether there was one in the first place. This is only possible by looking at the evidence which was presented in order to determine whether or not there is a marriage to be dissolved. The facts are contained in the various pieces of evidence and material presented to the committee of the other place. Very briefly I should like to refer to the proof of marriage. The petitioner, who was under oath, was asked by the clerk of the committee of the other place about her name, age, occupation and the like. These are the specific questions and answers:
Q. Are you married, and if so to whom?
A. I am, to Jan Paul Hankowski.

We have ahead of us some 700 similar bills seeking to do precisely the same thing, to dissolve a marriage or annul it, as the case may be. There is only one way whereby we can avoid having to consider these bills in the manner in which we now are. Even though our hopes were shattered many times in the past, we can hope again that the government will take action and some decision will be made thereby doing away with the necessity of having to rise and speak on a particular bill as I am now doing, even though I have no great desire to do so. Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose second reading of this bill and I desire to make clear to you and the house why I do so. I do not do so because I am opposed in principle to the dissolution of marriage, at least as a civil matter, nor do I do so because I have any knowledge of the facts of this particular case and the particular bill now before the house other than the facts recited in the bill itself. The house resumed at 8 p.m.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Nowlan for the second reading of Bill No. C-78, to amend the Income Tax Act.

When the order of business changed at five o'clock I was about to suggest that there are three important respects in which the bill to amend the Income Tax Act which is now before us perpetuates a long standing discrimination against those whose income is gained from wages and salaries. This discrimination applies with respect to amounts which are considered deductible from a taxpayer's income and relate to incidental
Income Tax Act
expenses incurred during the course of earning a living, the cost of board and lodging should an individual be required because of his employment to be absent from the place where he maintains his normal establishment, deductions for travelling expenses and, in the case of many skilled workers in this country, deductions in respect of the purchase and replacement of tools which they must use in their occupation.
This is a subject which I have raised a number of times when bills to amend the Income Tax Act have been before the house, and the question has been discussed on various occasions in this house in the past. I want to say that in my view those Canadians whose incomes arise from wages and salaries and who constitute, I suggest, the vast majority of our Canadian citizens, are not averse to being placed in a position where they cannot claim deductions in respect of many of these things, provided the same treatment is given to all other Canadian citizens. However, as we all know, that is not the situation which exists, and in some cases these deductions are allowed. My view is that the rules should apply fairly and equitably to all.
There are times, of course, when those who feel they are being discriminated against become restive and, indeed, they have probably sought the advice of friendly lawyers to assist them in getting round the problem which faces them. The bill has the effect of alleviating, and in some cases reducing, taxation generally and of providing certain other alleged benefits to taxpayers. I say "alleged" because some of my colleagues have questioned how effective they will be. I must say that we feel rather sorry, although I am not going to labour this point, sir, that instead of this bill, which was conceived in sin last April and was never allowed to be born, instead of this-well, I do not think I will continue that figure of

speech, because the hon. member tor Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) might want the page boys removed if I were to do so. But at any rate, this rather tired measure is all that is before us. We would have been much happier if those long range policies which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), on that day of repentance, June 24, envisaged, had actually seen the light of day five months later; but they have not.
All we have here is the residue of the late minister of finance. It is not very edifying. It is not very big. It is not very important. But it is, as I say, something like motherhood, which we are all in favour of, namely an alleviation of taxation as soon as possible. Therefore, it would seem to me, sir, that in accepting the principle of the bill, I should like to let the minister, who has got off pretty easily in these debates so far, know that we are not accepting all of its contents. He had a pretty easy time last Monday because it was a holiday; but when we get into committee on this bill we will expect the minister to tell us what all these clauses really mean and what their effect is going to be; and we will expect him to have all the answers.

speechtext:
I do not intend to speak at any length, Mr. Speaker, but I am very glad that we have attained this position anyway where the debate on the alleged general purpose of the bill is now concluded and that we shall be dealing with the sections. In response to the question from my friend the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) dealing with a certain section and the one from my friend across the chamber dealing with another subject, may I say that these matters will be dealt with when we come to these clauses in the committee, and that I do not intend to refer to them specifically at this time.
Naturally I have listened to the debate with interest. I think it has been a relatively good debate. I greatly appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Davenport although, like the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), I think it was, I found it to be a very difficult job to interpret the logic or the alleged logic which supposedly sewed together his remarks with very loose threads.
I assure my friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), that I realize I have not been mistreated by the house and, in fact, I will let him in on a deep and dark secret. I do not know all the answers to the sections, just as the hon. member for Davenport said this afternoon that he did not; and if the member for Bonavista-Twillingate thinks we are going to continue this debate until I can give satisfactory answers to every question, then I think the house will still be

dealing with this bill when we adjourn lor Christmas. However, I hope that will not be the situation.
I agree completely with what the hon. member for Davenport said at the outset of his remarks about the Income Tax Act having become very complicated and very technical, and I must admit that as minister of national revenue for some four years and somewhat responsible for the administration of the act I sometimes found it very difficult to understand or interpret. He said that this situation has grown worse throughout the years and in that regard I could not agree more if I were to adopt the language with respect to the act which the hon. member used in the earlier part of his comments this afternoon. This is inevitable, of course, and I think the same thing has been said in every parliament in the world in which they have income tax legislation, because obviously, as the act continues to develop in impact, you also get pressures and the necessity for creating exemptions and, unfortunately, you get the obvious necessity of sometimes using very technical language.
I have used the same argument myself in days gone by when I was sitting somewhere else than where I am now. I used to say: "Why can you not use simple, plain language which any farmer would understand and there would be no difficulty whatsoever if you did"? If that happened I would point out to those hon. members who have been complaining today about the loopholes which might possibly develop through which one might drive a coach and four, the result unfortunately would be that you could drive a tank through the act and there would be no loopholes but rather a complete morass. Therefore it is necessary, and no one knows this better than the hon. member for Davenport, to have technical language, and sometimes language with regard to which, as he said, even he has had to consult experts in order to understand it. I must confess I have also had to do that more than once, and after having retained one expert and then another who could not agree I thought the situation was even worse than I had understood it was at the outset. Be that as it may, unfortunately that is the framework of a very technical act and I make no apologies for it. I am sure that anyone in this chamber who has had the experience of dealing with taxation matters, and I know there are many hon. gentlemen here who have, regrets the necessity of using such language but also appreciates the fact that if it were not used the difficulties would sometimes be worse than the ones of which they complain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are introducing amendments now to the act and I have no doubt that other amendments, some perhaps substantial, will be introduced from time to time, but certainly we are not intending to have a complete revision and rewriting of the act at any time in the immediate future.
My hon. friend spoke about anomalies, and who would not do so? Of course there are anomalies in this act. No one knows that better than the hon. member for Davenport or myself, as far as that is concerned. We both have had some experience in dealing with them. There undoubtedly are some loopholes in the act. There were many, and many of them have been cured, I think, by amendments, though sometimes the amendment which cured the loophole perhaps created another one. That has been the history of income tax legislation and it is inevitable.
My hon. friend suggested that the clause dealing with incentives was loose, that it was one which would be impossible to administer and one which would create many difficulties. I admit it will create difficulties. No one who has had any responsibility for

Income Tax Act
the administration of the income tax law or any experience with it would deny that. But my hon. friend says that it is very easy and much simpler to do something else. He said, for instance, that we could allow a 100 per cent write-off in a year for plant and equipment and that would be a very simple incentive. But if all the firms investing in capital equipment were allowed to take a 100 per cent write-off in a year I wonder where the Minister of Finance would find the money with which to pay the hon. member for Davenport his indemnity. Whatever complaint there may have been about deficits during the last few years, I can understand that if that principle were followed the deficits that would ensue would be much greater than anything this country has ever known before, and I suggest that the difficulties of preventing that would be much greater than the difficulties of administering the section dealing with incentives.
The hon. member also referred to the fact that we should offer encouragement in surplus labour areas. That was provided for in the act two years ago, of course, and although it has not been as successful as one would like I think it has achieved some purpose in that field. The hon. member made other suggestions but I am not going to take up the time of the house tonight in dealing with them because I think they can be dealt with much better in the committee stage when I am sure the hon. member will raise them again. In one breath we are told that these incentives are no good at all and will result in nothing, and yet the suggestion is also made in the next breath that because of these incentives we are going to get corporate reorganizations and tens of thousands of dollars in legal fees are going to be spent to accomplish something which we are told is worth nothing at all. It just does not add up to logical common sense. As I said, I think it is much better to leave specific objections to the clauses to the committee stage, when we will be dealing with the clauses themselves.
The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) dealt with some general criticisms of the Income Tax Act and of this bill with which I agree entirely. He also suggested that he thought that any incentives which we have outlined here should be confined to Canadian corporations and not be made available to corporations under American control. That is a very good theory but one on which I would not want to comment at length tonight except to say it is very difficult to administer these particular provisions of the Income Tax Act with that motivation in view. I think there is some merit in some of the arguments which he has advanced. However, I do suggest to him that that is not the purpose of this section.

The purpose is not to control the ownership of corporations. The purpose of clause 10, the incentive clause, is to have businessmen go ahead and develop their trade, either export or local. I agree with my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it will have an impact. We have been assured by businessmen all over Canada that it will be helpful. However, it is not a solution to all the country's problems or anything of that kind. I think it will help to develop the Canadian economy.
I suggest to the hon. member for Lapointe if that is the purpose of the section, and it is not to control the ownership of corporations either United States or Canadian, but to develop the Canadian economy, to increase employment, then it does not make much difference to the people who are being employed at the moment whether the corporation is controlled in Canada or outside of Canada. What we were looking for in this incentive section is a way of increasing employment and increasing Canadian production. This other problem to which the hon. member referred is a very pertinent and very important problem, one with which we are all conversant and we are all concerned and no one more concerned than this government; but I suggest with respect to my hon. friend it cannot be dealt with through this section of the Income Tax Act which is before us.
Now, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) used the old, hackneyed expressions, the old catch phrases, to which we are so accustomed. He said that this was something to help the rich and not to help the poor. I did not apologize to the hon. member because I knew it was not necessary, but I had to leave for a few minutes while he was speaking. I think he made some reference to the fact that if 80,000 Canadians were being exempted from income tax because of that one amendment, that did not make this bill of any more assistance to the poor. It simply meant that there were too many poor people in this country. If that is logic, then I do not know what the term means. It may be that there are too many poor people in the country. I certainly sometimes feel that I have been included in that group throughout the whole of my lifetime and I would agree that there were too many of us and we were too poor. If we have an act that removes 80,000 taxpayers from the rolls at one stroke and then the hon. member says that this is no help, then I say that is not dealing with the situation frankly or honestly. I say this with all due respect to the hon. gentleman.
There are other clauses in this bill as well, as my hon. friend well knows. There is the clause to which the hon. member for

Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald) referred a few minutes ago, the one which permits the transfer of funds from pension funds to profit-sharing funds without having to pay income tax. There may be some wealthy people engaged in that area, and there probably are. I suggest to my hon. friend, who has very wide experience in the labour movement, who knows the law and particularly the economy of Ontario much better than I do, that the number of people who would be transferring from a pension fund to a profit-sharing fund would not include those about whom he was complaining, namely the very wealthy. I suggest it would be better in dealing with these matters to look at the situation frankly and deal with it on that basis rather than making appeals to prejudice and to class.
I rather regretted also the fact that this afternoon the hon. member saw fit to refer to some purported evidence that was brought in before a parliamentary group in another country the day before yesterday referring to two Canadian corporations. The hon. member for Lapointe may question whether they are Canadian corporations. The reference was to International Nickel and Falconbridge. These corporations were under attack the day before yesterday in a certain jurisdiction. After hearing the evidence that was brought in, so I am told, the chairman of one of these parliamentary committees today rather apologized for the attack which had been made basely and unfairly on these Canadian corporations. I regret the fact that these attacks were necessary in order to bolster a case about this act being for the benefit of the rich and to the detriment of the poor. I have no brief for either corporation, and I hold no shares in either one. All I know is that they are Canadian corporations and, according to reports today, the parliamentary group before which they were attacked reported they had been unfairly attacked. The statements made in another capital today would lead one to that conclusion. I regret, as I say, that my hon. friend saw fit to draw this matter into this debate.
After all, this is a rather humdrum debate dealing with certain technical sections, largely administrative, which, with the four exceptions I mentioned this afternoon, the ones dealing with incentives, and the oil and gas industry, are not likely to lead to an earth shaking debate in which philosophies are created or parties made or wrecked. I hope the house will now resolve itself into committee so that we can go ahead and deal with the bill before us section by section. I repeat what I said to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I do not want 27507-3-107i

On clause 1-Right to take petroleum or natural gas.

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of clause 1 of Bill No. C-78 I believe, and I ask the minister for information in this connection, is to assure that the receipt by a taxpayer in consideration for the disposition of a right, licence or privilege to explore for, drill for or take petroleum or natural gas in Canada, as provided by subsection (5b) or (5c) of section 83A, is included in the income of a taxpayer. This difficulty, I think, arises because of the fact that under the Income Tax Act there is no definition under section 3 of income as such. We have to stretch the situation under the Canadian Income Tax Act.
Section 3 of the Income Tax Act simply says "income" is income and includes income from property, employment and business. When the Income Tax Act was first introduced it was very simple for a man to determine his income because income was determined according to ordinary business principles. However, with the development of our act and income tax acts in other countries the meaning of income as such has become quite different from business income.
I would suggest that although it is necessary to pass this clause in order to bring this particular item within the gamut of income as defined under the act, we should look very seriously at section 3 of the act and consider the possibility of moving back to business principles in the determination of income, rather than be always moving further and further away and having to bring in, under section 6 of the act, items which under ordinary business principles would not be included as income of the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I can do no better at this time, Mr. Chairman, and I do not want to go too far afield. This is technical language which I am going to read for a moment from the technical explanation which I have in front of me. As I said earlier, this is a relieving amendment and I am sure my hon. friend knows that a taxpayer, under general law, cannot deduct expenses incurred in earning exempted income. If a taxpayer is earning income which is exempt from taxation then the taxpayer cannot deduct the expense of earning that income from his income.
Since a large part, or almost all of a holding company's income, consists of dividends from subsidiary companies, and since these dividends are exempt, the holding company, under general rule, would not be permitted to deduct the expenses involved. However, for many years-there is nothing new in this-the act has provided an exception to the general rule for those holding companies that could meet the test that more than 50 per cent of their income consisted of (a) shares

in capital stock and (b) bonds, debentures and mortgages of a subsidiary corporation controlled by them.
This amendment adds to these exceptions which I have read, and which have been in the law for years, a provision covering property leased to a subsidiary, and this will make it easier for holding companies to qualify for the exemptions which are permitted by deducting expenses in connection with their controlled subsidiaries.
As the hon. member for Davenport said this afternoon, it is very difficult to put this into simple language, but there is no departure from principle here. This deals with companies drawing income from subsidiaries and because of the fact that that income is exempt from taxation those companies could not deduct certain expenses.
What kind of property would be leased by a holding company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I do not know what property might be leased. I suppose anything could be leased from a warehouse to an automobile. Leasehold property would generally apply to leasehold real estate but, for instance, it would cover the expenses of the holding of a company meeting of the subsidiary, and company meetings, as my hon. friend knows, have to be held under statute at least once a year. That is one type of expense which is not permitted today and which would be permitted under this clause. Also if dividends are going to be paid, the expenses of issuing dividends and the printing of dividend cheques would be permitted, together with the corporate fees, the filing fees, of such a subsidiary. This is the type of expense involved and there would not be anything in it of major proportions. The clause covers the general operating expenses of subsidiaries in this case.
This is not embarking on any new principle. It is something which had been recommended on more than one occasion. I received these briefs from time to time when I was minister of national revenue and I am sure my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River heard them before. When this resolution was first put forward, I wonder whether there was any thought at that time-this was on April 10 I believe-that shortly afterwards the Canadian dollar might be devalued and hence might result in some very substantial windfall profits to a great many companies who probably never expected them? I wonder if the minister would answer that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer is no.

If the answer is no, Mr. Chairman, then I wonder if the minister is still as convinced that this proposal is in the form in which it should become the law of this country?
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I admit it is quite possible that the results of clause 10 in the amendments to the income tax bill will surprise the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan).
As an incentive to production at this time, the minister would like to offer 50 per cent tax exemptions on production increases. I think the minister will experience an unpleasant surprise at the results, for if we
Income Tax Act
look at the facts at the present time, in Canada we realize that the production is not even sold because the Canadian people do not have the required purchasing power.
So, what is the good of promising tax reductions as a production incentive when producers, manufacturers and industrialists have already on hand a pile-up of stocks in warehouses and manufactures.
How can we promise tax reductions to producers as a production incentive when last year's production is not even disposed of? You only have to visit our stores and our manufactures of shoes, suits, shirts or even our house builders to see that they have the capacity to increase their production by 200 per cent.
As a matter of fact, our manufactures of white furniture, stoves, refrigerators, washing machines, operate at only 40 per cent of their capacity. These manufactures would produce more even if their taxes were not reduced, but if the citizens of Canada were able, through an increased purchasing power, to buy that furniture.
The Canadian manufacturers are able to produce more even if section 10 is not added to the bill.
I fail to see whom these exemptions would benefit. Especially at the present time, excluding a few exceptions, how could our Canadian industries and manufactures benefit from them, since they voluntarily reduce their production because it does not sell?
If the Minister of Finance wants to increase production, he should, in my opinion, start by increasing the purchasing power of the citizens of Canada.
(Text):

I should like to refer to the matter raised by the hon. member for Davenport, and may I amplify it slightly to the minister. This section was designed to be an incentive to production, but consideration is not given to the fact that even with no production at all those sectors of our economy, manufacturing and processing, which are making exactly the same output as they did prior to devaluation have been given this great benefit resulting from devaluation of the dollar recommended by this government and have been given a production incentive bonus as well. They do not need to increase their production because they have already had a benefit, which in some industries has amounted to many millions of dollars, but on top of that they are to receive the additional benefit of a reduction in tax.
I wonder if the minister is in a position to give us any idea what this proposal is going

Income Tax Act
to cost the public treasury? It seems to me that this is another illustration of what has been referred to as taking from those in the lower income bracket and giving to those in the higher income bracket, in this case corporations which in many instances are owned by non-residents. I think if we could introduce one other scriptural quotation it would be, "By their fruits shall ye know them."

If I understood the Minister of Finance correctly when he replied in the debate on second reading, he said that there were safeguards in this amendment against abuse of it by those who would seek to get this benefit by merely raising prices. Also, if I understood him correctly, he seemed to suggest that the wording of the amendment would prevent the benefit of a tax concession accruing to a corporation or a firm which was merely taking sales from another firm instead of benefiting the total economy through increased production.
I have not been able to find any such language. I may have missed it, and I should be grateful if the minister could now, if he would, with the help of the experts in front of him, tell the committee and in that way tell me, what language there is in this clause which would prevent its abuse in the two ways mentioned, namely merely increases in prices and by switching sales from A to B or from B to A in the economy. Would the minister like to answer that query, as perhaps I missed the language.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall reply later.

Referring to clause 10, which I would take as the kernel or core of the tax incentive legislation before the house, I would suggest to the minister that a lot of the sting of the incentive is lost in what I might term a mass of paper. For example, Mr. Chairman, if you look at the illustration given on page 7 you see that in producing a sales increase from $900,000 to $1 million a company achieves a tax saving of about $1,230. I would suggest that it would scarcely be worth while for an average corporation or average taxpayer to negotiate their way through this legislation to achieve a tax saving of $1,230.
The second point I wish to make is that a great deal of the incentive of this legislation will be lost by reason of the fact that you have a flexible advantage to the taxpayer. In other words, the better you do this year the less chance you will have of getting an incentive next year, and that is a serious handicap to the legislation.
The third point I would like to bring to the minister's attention is that the provision applies only to corporations. It does not apply to sole proprietorships and unincorporated

partnerships, and perhaps when the minister concludes his remarks on this clause he would tell us why it is that only corporations are to have the benefit of the tax credit.
The fourth point I offer for the minister's consideration is that the eligible taxpayers under this measure are confined to manufacturing and processing corporations. Therefore this will in effect exclude all retail and servicing establishments, and here again I think the incentives are unnecessarily confined.

Could the minister tell the committee what we have in Canada that is in short supply and that these incentives will help us to produce? I would also like him to tell us whether he does not think that these incentives will produce a situation where high pressure salesmanship is going to be applied thus causing people to put themselves in debt to finance companies. Under pressure of salesmanship people will put themselves in the position of buying things on time and mortgaging their future, and I do not know that there are so many things in short supply at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak for the remaining couple of minutes in order that the minister may have time to think over the questions asked. First of all I would like to say that all of us on this side of the house are in favour of incentives as such, whether they be incentives to manufacturing industries, corporations or individuals. I would not like to make the distinction which was made by the hon. member for York South this afternoon because I believe that many Canadian corporations, at least those which are Canadian owned, are made up of Canadian individuals, and if these corporations can be given incentives to produce more jobs at a reasonable cost to the taxpayers, and without causing a great change in the distribution of income tax in favour of those in the higher income levels, then those incentives should be encouraged.
However, there are many criticisms which can be made with regard to this particular clause which is to introduce a new section 40A into the Income Tax Act, as it is written at the moment. First of all this type of incentive encourages firms to increase prices, regardless of what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said this afternoon. We are not operating in an economy which is absolutely free and in which prices are determined on an interplay of market forces. In some instances people do have something to say with regard to determination of the prices of their products, and they will have something to say in particular cases regarding determination of their prices under this legislation in order to obtain tax benefits. There is no doubt

about that. Another thing which is bad about this particular clause is that it does not present any incentive for efficiency within an industry.
Suppose we have an industrial producer who is selling all he can sell in existing markets in Canada, but who can come along and operate more efficiently and at a lower price which might help him in the export market. He is given no incentive on additional profits which are made through lowering costs in his manufacturing concern.
Clause 10 stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the house will do tomorrow; and perhaps the house leader would be good enough to indicate what we will be doing next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to outline the work for tomorrow and all of next week, subject to any unforeseen circumstances. The intention is to proceed steadily with legislation and we will continue with the four bills under the Minister of Finance until they are concluded, starting tomorrow with the one we are on now, which would be the first item. The second would be Bill C-79 concerning the Estate Tax Act, the third would be the Excise Tax Act and the fourth the Customs Tariff Act.
I will list the other items to which the house might direct its attention, reserving the right to change the order after we conclude the four bills I have mentioned. These are Bill C-4, an act to amend the Department of National Health and Welfare Act, which we were debating the other day, and
Business of the House
Bill C-71, an act to amend the Farm Credit Act, which is close to being finished.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What number is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is No. 2. Then there will appear in Votes and Proceedings tomorrow, and on Monday's order paper three resolutions, two of which refer to items mentioned in the speech from the throne-a national economic development board and the Atlantic development board, together, perhaps, with a short resolution dealing with an amendment to the act which set up the productivity council.
In addition to those items, we shall consider the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Transport dealing with the Freight Rates Reduction Act and then the resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance dealing with C.N.R. capital expenditures; the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with a manpower consultative service; then Bill No. C-64 dealing with an amendment to the Coal Production Assistance Act-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have gone far enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Some of these are small, of course, though most of them are of major importance. Afterwards we shall take the resolution dealing with the Aeronautics Act and the resolution in the name of the Minister of Justice dealing with an amendment to the Judges Act, followed by Bill No. C-70 in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with the safety of persons in federal works.
I missed one out of our list-Bill No. C-49 dealing with an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act.
It being five minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
